newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Sarajevo turns clocks back, others don't.
newsitem.headline: Sarajevo turns clocks back, others don't.

text.p: In a country where the most innocent issue can become a source of ethnic dispute, Bosnia's Moslems, Serbs and Croats now can't agree on what time it is.
By government decree, clocks were set back an hour on Sunday in Moslem-controlled parts of Bosnia.
The rest of the country -- and surrounding areas of western Europe -- stuck with the old time.
So when Sarajevans sat down for Sunday lunch at noon, watches in the Serb republic town of Pale a few kilometres (miles) away read one o'clock.
In the ethnically divided city of Mostar, Croats on the west bank of the Neretva river were an hour ahead of Moslems on the east bank.
This despite the fact that Moslems and Croats are partners in a federation governing 51 per cent of Bosnia.

"If this is a preview of what we can expect from a unified Bosnia I think the country might be better off going back to war," joked one Sarajevan who was at a loss to explain how or why his government had decided to go it alone on a time change.
Because it was Sunday, no one was available at the Ministry of Social Policy, which made the decision, to justify the wisdom of its policy.
"I didn't even realize there was a time-change difficulty until reporters rang me up about it," said Major Simon Haselock, a NATO spokesman in Sarajevo.
"If there are two times in Bosnia it would certainly be confusing. We turned our clocks back here at the headquarters."
Officials contacted in Croat and Serb-controlled parts of Bosnia said they would wait until late October and set their clocks back along with the rest of western Europe.
"Would you rather be in step with Europe or in step with the Moslems in Sarajevo?" said one Croat official in Mostar who asked not to be named.
Businessmen in Sarajevo were exasperated, saying the time differences could complicate their daily arrangements in other parts of Bosnia and in neighbouring countries.
"Somebody obviously was not thinking about the consequences before making such a stupid decision," complained 30-year-old Senad Alic.
"It affects me because I do a lot of business in Zagreb (Croatia) where the time is now different."
